title: What is the Actor model as used by Akka? Explain private state, asynchronous immutable messages, the mailbox, how it eliminates shared mutable state, and the trade-offs versus locks.

s1_definition.profdef: The Actor model is a concurrency paradigm where the unit of computation is an actor: an object that encapsulates private mutable state no one else can touch, communicates only by sending asynchronous immutable messages, and processes those messages one at a time from a mailbox. Because each actor handles exactly one message at a time and nothing else can read or write its state, there is no shared mutable state and therefore no need for locks. Akka is a JVM implementation that schedules many lightweight actors over a small thread pool. The trade-off versus locks is that actors eliminate data races and deadlocks by design but introduce message-passing latency, eventual-consistency style reasoning, and the need to handle supervision and backpressure.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine each account at National Bank of India has its own dedicated clerk who alone can touch that account's ledger. Nobody else ever writes in the ledger. If you want something done, you drop a written request into the clerk's in-tray (the mailbox), and the clerk handles requests one at a time, in order. Since only one clerk ever touches each ledger and only ever one request at a time, two people can never corrupt the balance, and there is no need for anyone to take turns with a shared key. That dedicated, single-threaded clerk with a private ledger and an in-tray is an actor.
s1_definition.oneliner: An actor owns private state, receives asynchronous immutable messages into a mailbox, and processes them one at a time, so shared mutable state and locks disappear entirely.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Actor model is a concurrency paradigm where the unit of computation is an actor: an object that encapsulates private mutable state no one else can touch, communicates only by sending asynchronous immutable messages, and processes those messages one at a time from a mailbox. Because each actor handles exactly one message at a time and nothing else can read or write its state, there is no shared mutable state and therefore no need for locks. Akka is a JVM implementation that schedules many lightweight actors over a small thread pool. The trade-off versus locks is that actors eliminate data races and deadlocks by design but introduce message-passing latency, eventual-consistency style reasoning, and the need to handle supervision and backpressure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine each account at National Bank of India has its own dedicated clerk who alone can touch that account's ledger. Nobody else ever writes in the ledger. If you want something done, you drop a written request into the clerk's in-tray (the mailbox), and the clerk handles requests one at a time, in order. Since only one clerk ever touches each ledger and only ever one request at a time, two people can never corrupt the balance, and there is no need for anyone to take turns with a shared key. That dedicated, single-threaded clerk with a private ledger and an in-tray is an actor.

**One line to remember:** An actor owns private state, receives asynchronous immutable messages into a mailbox, and processes them one at a time, so shared mutable state and locks disappear entirely.

sections.s2_technical:
An actor encapsulates private mutable state that is never exposed. No other thread or actor can read or write that state directly. The only way to interact is to send the actor a message. Because the actor processes exactly one message at a time, its internal state mutations are automatically safe without any lock, since there is never concurrent access to that state.

Messages must be immutable. When actor A sends a message to actor B, the message should carry only immutable data, so that after sending, A cannot mutate something B is about to read. In Akka you model messages as immutable classes or records, for example a `Deposit(amount)` record. Immutability is what guarantees that passing a message between threads is safe, because there is nothing shared that can change underneath the receiver.

Message sending is asynchronous and lands in the receiver's mailbox, a queue of pending messages. The sender does not block; it fires the message and continues. The actor's dispatcher assigns a thread to the actor only when it has messages to process, runs the actor's behavior for one message, then frees the thread. This is why Akka can run millions of actors over a handful of threads: actors are cheap, and threads are shared cooperatively rather than one-per-actor.

Eliminating shared mutable state is the whole point. Traditional lock-based concurrency has many threads touching shared objects, so you must guard every access with locks, and getting the locking wrong causes data races or deadlocks. In the Actor model there is nothing shared to guard. Each actor is a serial island. Coordination happens by sending messages, not by sharing memory, which is often summarized as "do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating."

A senior-level nuance is the trade-offs. Actors remove data races and deadlocks by construction and scale well across cores and even across machines with location transparency, and Akka adds supervision hierarchies so a failing actor can be restarted by its parent. But you pay with message-passing latency, you must reason about eventual ordering and at-most-once or at-least-once delivery, mailboxes can grow unbounded so you need backpressure, and debugging asynchronous message flows is harder than a straight call stack. Actors shine for high-concurrency, stateful, event-driven systems; a simple short critical section may still be cleaner with a lock.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes concurrent deposits and withdrawals against the same account from many channels at once. With shared state and locks, the team kept hitting race conditions and the occasional deadlock when two accounts were locked in different orders. This is exactly what the Actor model fixes — give each account its own actor with private state so only one message is ever processed at a time and no lock is needed.

Problem 2 — Requests arrive faster than they can be handled during spikes, and messages must be queued fairly and processed in order per account. This is exactly what the mailbox provides — a per-actor queue processed one message at a time.

Because Akka is an external library, the demo builds a small educational actor that mirrors Akka's design: an `AccountActor` with private balance, an immutable message type, a mailbox backed by a blocking queue, and a single processing thread that handles one message at a time. The demo sends deposits and withdrawals to Rajesh's and Priya's account actors concurrently and shows safe, lock-free, in-order processing.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh's actor opens at 1,000,000; several sender threads fire five deposits of 1000 and five withdrawals of 500 concurrently; Priya's actor receives one deposit of 75,000.

Step 1 — Each account gets its own actor running on its own thread. Rajesh's balance lives only inside his actor; nobody else can touch it.

Step 2 — The sender threads call `tell`, which simply enqueues immutable messages into Rajesh's mailbox and returns immediately. The senders never block and never touch the balance.

Step 3 — Rajesh's actor thread takes one message at a time from the mailbox. Because it is strictly serial, two messages never mutate the balance at the same time, so no lock is needed even though many senders are firing concurrently.

Step 4 — The actor applies each message: five deposits add 5,000, five withdrawals subtract 2,500, leaving 1,002,500. Priya's actor independently applies its deposit, moving 250,000 to 325,000.

Step 5 — Each actor receives a STOP message, finishes draining, and exits. The balances are correct and consistent, achieved with zero locks and zero shared mutable state.

Final output:

```
INFO: SAV2001 deposit 1000 → balance 1001000
INFO: SAV2001 withdraw 500 → balance 1000500
... (processed serially, interleaved per mailbox order)
INFO: CUR3001 deposit 75000 → balance 325000
Rajesh final balance: 1002500
Priya final balance:  325000
```

  │       mutates PRIVATE balance (no lock, serial)         │

  ┌──────────────── AccountActor "CUR3001" ────────────────┐
  │  MAILBOX: [dep 75000] → balance 250000 → 325000         │

  No shared mutable state between actors → no races, no deadlocks.
```

  │  + run()      (one at a time) │        └──────────────────────────┘
  │  - handle(msg)                │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Message Handling ───────────────────────

  [IDLE] ──message arrives──→ [PROCESSING one msg] ──done──→ [IDLE]
                                   │ STOP
                                   ▼
                              [TERMINATED]

  ── Trade-offs vs Locks ───────────────────────────────────
   Actors: no races/deadlocks by design, scales, supervised
           BUT message latency, eventual ordering, mailbox backpressure
   Locks:  direct, low-latency for short critical sections
           BUT easy to deadlock, hard to scale, races if misused

  Contract for tell():
    Pre:  message immutable
    Post: enqueued to mailbox; processed serially later
    Guarantee: single-threaded state access → lock-free safety
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Actor model is a concurrency approach where the unit of work is an actor, which is an object that holds private mutable state nobody else can touch, communicates only by sending asynchronous immutable messages, and processes those messages one at a time from a queue called a mailbox. Because each actor handles exactly one message at a time and nothing else can read or write its state, there is no shared mutable state and therefore no need for locks at all. Akka is the main JVM implementation, and it schedules millions of lightweight actors over a small thread pool, assigning a thread to an actor only when it has messages to process.

The three pillars are private state, immutable messages, and the mailbox. The private state means the actor's data is a serial island that only its own single thread ever mutates, so those mutations are automatically safe. The messages must be immutable so that once I send one, I cannot change something the receiver is about to read, which is what makes passing data between threads safe. The mailbox is the per-actor queue; sending is asynchronous, so the sender just enqueues the message and continues without blocking, and the actor drains the mailbox one message at a time, which naturally serializes all access to its state.

This eliminates shared mutable state, which is the root cause of data races and deadlocks in lock-based concurrency. Instead of many threads touching shared objects behind locks, actors coordinate purely by sending messages, often summarized as sharing memory by communicating rather than communicating by sharing memory. The trade-offs are real, though. Actors remove races and deadlocks by construction, scale across cores and even machines with location transparency, and Akka adds supervision so a parent can restart a failed actor. But I pay with message-passing latency, I have to reason about eventual ordering and delivery guarantees, mailboxes can grow unbounded so I need backpressure, and asynchronous flows are harder to debug than a plain call stack. For a tiny short critical section, a simple lock can still be cleaner.

At National Bank of India we had concurrent deposits and withdrawals hitting the same accounts from many channels, and with shared state and locks we kept getting race conditions and the occasional deadlock from inconsistent lock ordering. We modeled each account as an actor with its own private balance and a mailbox, so every command becomes an immutable message that the account's single thread processes one at a time, which removed the locks entirely and made the deadlocks impossible by design. The sentence I give interviewers is that the Actor model gives each actor private state, asynchronous immutable messages, and a mailbox processed one message at a time, which eliminates shared mutable state so there are no locks, and the trade-off versus locking is that I gain race-free, deadlock-free scalability at the cost of message latency, eventual ordering, and backpressure concerns.
